source: Bazigaran & Sohn (2025) Concept Generalization in Humans and LLMs: the Number Game
finding: GPT-o1-mini was compared with human number-game data (Tenenbaum 1999 paradigm) and a Bayesian model. The Bayesian model fit humans better than it fit the LLM. The LLM did not generalise from one example.
numbers: 255 example sets, targets 1-100, 10 trials averaged. Mean JSD: human-Bayes 0.36, GPT-Bayes 0.56 (baseline model).
limits: One model (o1-mini) in the main analysis; short NeurIPS 2025 workshop paper; hypothesis space holds only primitive math rules.
agent_relevance: In S2 REPRESENT a model may anchor on the given example and not propose a broader rule. Ask for several candidate rules, not one.

source: Bazigaran & Sohn (2025) Concept Generalization in Humans and LLMs: the Number Game (rule bias)
finding: Fitting the rule-vs-interval prior shows the LLM is more rule-biased than humans. Humans mix rule and similarity concepts. The LLM leans on rules.
numbers: Best-fit rule bias: humans 0.9, GPT 1.0 (baseline 0.5). Fit improved divergence: human-Bayes 0.36 to 0.30, GPT-Bayes 0.56 to 0.49.
limits: Rule bias is read from a fitted parameter, so it depends on the Bayesian hypothesis space chosen.
agent_relevance: Our agent may over-prefer crisp rules and under-use similarity or interval reasoning. S7 should check whether a similarity reading also fits.

source: Bazigaran & Sohn (2025) Concept Generalization in Humans and LLMs: the Number Game (ablation)
finding: Ablating Bayesian parts showed the LLM acts like a maximum-likelihood learner. Humans act like prior plus hypothesis averaging.
numbers: Variant divergence (human/GPT): MAP 0.60/0.50, BinL 0.33/0.65, MaxL 0.66/0.42. Human best variant BinL, worst MaxL. GPT best MaxL, worst BinL. GPT-Bayes gap shrinks with 4 examples to near the human-Bayes level.
limits: Post hoc explanation; the authors say a memory-capacity story is untested.
agent_relevance: Suggests forcing multi-hypothesis averaging in S7 (keep several rules alive) instead of picking one best rule early.

source: Bazigaran & Sohn (2025) Concept Generalization in Humans and LLMs: the Number Game (other LLMs)
finding: GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3 and LLaMA-3-8B showed weaker, less structured generalisation than o1-mini.
numbers: Qualitative only, no table in main text.
limits: No numbers; appendix figures only.
agent_relevance: A reasoning model did better than plain chat models on concept generalisation. Reasoning-style scaffolds may help S2.

source: Ellis (2023) Human-like Few-Shot Learning via Bayesian Reasoning over Natural Language (NeurIPS 2023)
finding: An LLM proposes candidate concepts in natural language. A prior and likelihood re-weight them. This fits human number-game judgments with 50-100 proposals.
numbers: Fit needs 50-100 proposals to match the average of 8 humans; the original number-game model used over 5000 hypotheses. Python-code prior fit worse than English prior. No-proposal ablation fit poorly.
limits: Prior tuned on human data; proposals come from Codex; GPT-4 alone judged very differently from humans.
agent_relevance: Closest published design to our S2 + S7: LLM proposes rules, a scoring step re-weights them. Use language rules, not code.

source: Ellis (2023) (logical concepts)
finding: On a logical-concept learning-curve task the model explained human responses far better than GPT-4 alone and came within 3 percent of human accuracy.
numbers: R2 = .81 with 100 proposals per batch. First-order prompt only: R2 = .80. The baseline Bayesian program learner needed about 10^9 proposals to do slightly worse.
limits: Tuned prior was critical; the pretrained prior was highly syntax-sensitive.
agent_relevance: The prior matters more than raw proposals. Our agent needs a plain plausibility check on rule wording (simple, natural rules first).

source: Ellis (2023) (GPT-4 alone)
finding: GPT-4 answering yes/no on number-game items gave judgments unlike humans, and was less accurate than the proposal-plus-Bayes model on logical concepts.
numbers: No number for the number game; on logical concepts below the 81 percent variance explained of the hybrid.
limits: Author notes there is no ground truth for the number-game items.
agent_relevance: Direct answering is a weaker route than explicit hypothesis scoring.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Inductive Reasoning with Hypothesis Refinement (ICLR 2024)
finding: GPT-4 proposing, testing and refining textual rules with a symbolic checker beat plain input-output prompting on 3 of 4 datasets.
numbers: ACRE raw accuracy: IO 64.0, self-refine 70.0, refine T=3 N=5 82.5; task accuracy 28.0 / 32.0 / 59.0. MiniARC raw: IO 33.1, refine 18.7 (worse). Majority vote over samples did not help (65.0 on ACRE).
limits: MiniARC is visual and text-only models do badly; symbolic interpreter is task specific; main model GPT-4 (GPT-3.5, Claude-2, LLaMA2-70B in appendix, weaker).
agent_relevance: Core pattern for S2/S7: propose, test against all examples with an external checker, refine. Self-check by the same LLM is much weaker.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) (rule application gap)
finding: The LLM proposes good rules but applies them badly, even its own rules. Replacing the symbolic checker by the LLM lowers accuracy.
numbers: ACRE task accuracy 59.0 with symbolic checker; MiniSCAN task accuracy falls from over 80 percent to near zero with the LM as interpreter (text of paper).
limits: Model GPT-4; tasks synthetic.
agent_relevance: In S7 (rules still fitting) do not ask the model to judge whether a rule fits; run the rule on each example as a separate step or with code.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) (brittleness)
finding: Induction is brittle to noisy examples and unfamiliar symbols. Humans tolerate a few errors. The LLM does not.
numbers: List Functions, 8 exemplars, 12.5 / 25 / 50 percent corrupted: accuracy fell at every step, even one bad example hurt. Telling the model about noise helped only partly. MiniSCAN accuracy dropped with pseudoword outputs.
limits: Noise was random swaps in outputs.
agent_relevance: Add a noise-tolerant fit rule in S7: allow one exception before dropping a rule, and say so in the prompt.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) (human comparison)
finding: Appendix gives human reference scores for the same datasets. Hypothesis refinement is not always above human level.
numbers: List Functions humans about 45.9 percent (Rule 2020); ARC humans about 80 percent of tasks; ConceptARC humans 90.9 percent.
limits: Authors say their own human study did not cover all LLM setups.
agent_relevance: Calibrate expectations per task before trusting a rule-induction loop.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models (ICLR 2024)
finding: GPT-4 writes many abstract hypotheses in language, then programs, then tests on examples. Summarising the hypotheses first helps.
numbers: ARC 100-task subset: direct prompting 17 percent, programs 23, with LLM-summarised hypotheses 30, human-picked hypotheses 33. Icecuber DSL solver 43 percent. 1D-ARC zero-shot hypotheses 71.3 vs two-shot 73.1. Chain-of-thought hypotheses without programs: 19 percent.
limits: Costly (many samples); SyGuS: direct programs already 94.3 percent, hypotheses added little; random 100-task ARC subset only.
agent_relevance: Supports a two-step S2: write several language rules, filter to a few, then test each. Hypotheses help most on hard tasks.

source: Parab et al. (2025) Error Sources in LLM-based Hypothesis Search for Few-Shot Rule Induction
finding: Hypothesis search matched humans on List Functions, and direct program generation (GPT-4o, Codex) lagged. Error analysis shows where it breaks.
numbers: Generator 46.4 percent correct hypotheses; Summarizer 34.5 (drops 26 percent of correct ones, 12.1 points overall loss); Implementor 61.2; overall test solve 62.0. Up to 257 LLM calls per task. Refinement rescued only 4.3 percent of semantically wrong hypotheses.
limits: Human data from the Rule 2020 task set; GPT-4o; costly.
agent_relevance: Summarising or merging candidate rules can throw away the right one. In S7 keep rules separate and score each, do not merge early.

source: Zhu et al. (2024) Large Language Models can Learn Rules (Hypotheses-to-Theories)
finding: An LLM induces rules from training examples, keeps only rules that are often right, and stores them as a rule library for later questions. This is explanation-based style knowledge reuse.
numbers: GPT-4: CLUTRR 5-shot CoT 50.6 to 64.3 (+13.7); base-16 arithmetic 57.4 to 78.4 (+21.0); List Functions raw 57.4 to 76.1, task 46.0 to 56.2. Rules from GPT-4 doubled GPT-3.5 task accuracy on List Functions to 34.4.
limits: Needs labelled training examples; GPT-3.5 sometimes fails to induce rules; random-answer-rule ablation shows rules must be correct.
agent_relevance: Model for agent memory: collect candidate rules, count when they lead to a right answer, keep those above a threshold. Transfers across models.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners (AAAI)
finding: An agent turns past success and failure trajectories into natural-language insights and reuses them with retrieval of similar tasks. No weight update.
numbers: HotpotQA 40 percent vs Reflexion 39 at round 3; ALFWorld 59 vs Reflexion 54 at round 3; insights transferred from HotpotQA to FEVER. Insights-only and retrieve-only variants were worse than both together.
limits: Table cells garbled in text extraction; GPT-3.5/4 backbones; gain smaller on WebShop.
agent_relevance: A working loop mixing exemplar memory (retrieve similar cases) with abstracted insight, like the exemplar-plus-rule mix seen in humans. Fits S2 and S7.

source: Wang, Shang & Zhong (2023) Goal-Driven Explainable Clustering via Language Descriptions (GoalEx)
finding: An LLM proposes cluster descriptions in words, assigns each text to descriptions, then an integer program picks a small, low-overlap set. Clusters follow the user's goal, not just topic.
numbers: Humans picked the PAS explanation 80 percent of the time vs 56 for LDA and 71 for Instructor. 66 percent of samples covered on average. PAS under Instructor by 11 percent on one dataset; improved 14 percent with a stronger model.
limits: Text corpora only; coverage not 100 percent by design.
agent_relevance: Clustering analogue of Anderson 1991 for LLMs: propose, assign, select. Useful when the agent must split examples into several sub-rules.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Hypothesis Generation with Large Language Models (HypoGeniC)
finding: A bandit-style loop (upper-confidence bound) generates hypotheses from few examples, scores them on training data and replaces weak ones. Hypotheses beat few-shot prompting.
numbers: Gains over few-shot: +31.7 SHOE SALES, +13.9 DECEPTIVE REVIEWS, +3.3 HEADLINE, +24.9 TWEET. Beat supervised learning by 12.1 and 11.6 on two sets. Updating the bank improved quality.
limits: Text classification; on DECEPTIVE REVIEWS fine-tuned models won on word cues.
agent_relevance: Exploration vs exploitation over a rule bank: test top rules on each new case, replace the ones that fail. Same shape as S7.

source: Jagadish et al. (2024) Ecologically rational meta-learned inference (ERMI), ICML
finding: LLM-generated tasks train a meta-learned network. It fits human category learning better than seven other models, including the Rational Model of Categorization (Anderson 1991), GCM and a prototype model.
numbers: Fit to Badham 2017: ERMI BIC 38722 vs Claude-2 direct 39817. Mean-squared error to Shepard curves: ERMI 0.05 vs Claude-2 0.18; learning-curve MSE vs RMC 0.10 and PFN 0.17 vs ERMI 0.03. OpenML-CC18 23 tasks: ERMI 70.95 percent accuracy vs TabPFN 70.51.
limits: Claude-2 simulated only via prompts; ERMI fails on one generalisation stimulus (T2); small tabular benchmark. RMC was a close second in fit.
agent_relevance: Anderson's clustering model still ranks near the top for human-like fit, so it is a fair reference for how flexible category learning looks.

source: Jagadish et al. (2024) (LLM as direct learner)
finding: Claude-2 prompted directly as a learner was fully exemplar-based after the second block, unlike humans and ERMI, who shift from prototype to exemplar use.
numbers: Devraj 2021 task BIC: ERMI 41207 vs Claude-2 42401. Prototype/exemplar error gap: ERMI 0.09 +-0.01 vs MI 0.17 +-0.02.
limits: One older model (Claude-2); prompt format may matter.
agent_relevance: A prompted LLM may just look up near copies of seen cases. Do not assume it forms a summary rule on its own.

source: Jagadish et al. (2024) (Shepard types replication)
finding: Replicated Shepard, Hovland & Jenkins (1961) type difficulty using Nosofsky 1994 (N = 120) and Badham 2017 (N = 96 adults aged 18-87) human data. Type II was harder than types III-V for the model, as for humans.
numbers: Nosofsky 1994 N=120; Badham 2017 N=96, first four types only.
limits: Human data reused from earlier papers, not a new run.
agent_relevance: Rule complexity (number of features in the rule) is a stable predictor of difficulty. Cheap check for our rule scoring.

source: Binz et al. (2023) Meta-Learned Models of Cognition
finding: Meta-learning can build Bayes-optimal learners without writing priors by hand, so rational models like Anderson's can be approximated by networks.
numbers: No single figure; framework paper reviewing earlier results.
limits: Skimmed; category-learning sections not read in full.
agent_relevance: Background for the ERMI line. Low direct use in a prompt-only agent.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Language Models as Inductive Reasoners (DEER)
finding: Introduces inducing natural-language rules from natural-language facts, with a 1.2k rule-fact dataset and a chain-of-language-models method.
numbers: DEER dataset 1.2k rule-fact pairs, 100 val and 200 test per setup; metrics precision, recall, F1, plus human scoring of consistency, reality, generality, non-triviality.
limits: Result table numbers not extracted in this session.
agent_relevance: Gives a rubric for scoring induced rules: consistent, true, general, non-trivial. Useful for S7 rule checks.

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning
finding: Rule-inducing (program) and direct-answer models solve different ARC problems. Combining them helps most.
numbers: ARC validation, 2 tries: ensemble 26.50 percent with GPT-4 descriptions; induction 18.78; transduction 15.25. With GPT-4o-mini descriptions: ensemble 19.50, induction 11.07, transduction 13.50.
limits: Trained models, not prompts; ARC only.
agent_relevance: Rule induction wins on precise composed concepts, direct judgement on fuzzy perceptual ones. Let S2 fall back to similarity answers.

source: Moskvichev, Odouard & Mitchell (2023) ConceptARC
finding: On 480 tasks over 16 concepts, humans far beat GPT-4 and two ARC programs, which suggests weak concept abstraction in machines.
numbers: Humans 91 percent; first-place Kaggle program 52; GPT-4 zero-shot 25 percent (0.19 at temp 0, 0.25 at temp 0.5); GPT-4 under 30 percent on 15 of 16 concepts. Humans over 90 on 11 of 16 concepts.
limits: GPT-4 text version, simple zero-shot prompt; 3 guesses allowed.
agent_relevance: Concept-group tests, not single tasks, show whether an inferred rule is truly general.

source: Mitchell, Palmarini & Moskvichev (2023) Comparing Humans, GPT-4, GPT-4V on Abstraction and Reasoning
finding: A more detailed one-shot prompt raised GPT-4 on ConceptARC text tasks, but still far below humans. GPT-4V on images was worse.
numbers: GPT-4 one-shot 0.33 at both temperatures vs 0.19 / 0.25 zero-shot. Minimal tasks (48): humans 0.95, GPT-4 text 0.69 (temp 0) / 0.65 (0.5), GPT-4V zero-shot 0.25, one-shot 0.23.
limits: Small 48-task set for the vision test; older models.
agent_relevance: Prompt detail gave about +8 to +14 points; the gap to humans stayed large. Prompting alone will not close it.

source: Anderson (1991) The adaptive nature of human categorization (Psychological Review)
finding: Rational model of categorization: items join an existing cluster or start a new one, with a prior favouring larger clusters (Chinese-restaurant style) and a likelihood from feature match. Not read this session; background only.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Cluster-or-new decision is a model for when S2 should add a new rule instead of stretching the old one.

source: Love, Medin & Gureckis (2004) SUSTAIN: a network model of category learning
finding: Clusters are added only when a surprising error occurs. Supervised and unsupervised learning use one mechanism. Not read this session.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Add a new sub-rule only after a surprising failure, the same trigger as S7 in our schema.

source: Mitchell, Keller & Kedar-Cabelli (1986) Explanation-Based Generalization: a unifying view (Machine Learning)
finding: Explanation-based generalisation builds a general rule from one example by proving why it fits with a domain theory. Not read this session.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened; classic limit is the need for a correct domain theory.
agent_relevance: One-shot rule from one example plus background knowledge: matches LLM-agent use of prior knowledge in S2. HtT and ExpeL above are soft versions.

source: Tenenbaum (1999) Rules and similarity in concept learning (NIPS)
finding: Number game: Bayes with a size principle explains rule-like and similarity-like generalisation from few examples. Known here only second hand from the 2023 and 2025 papers read above.
numbers: Second hand: human data from Bigelow & Piantadosi 2016, at least 9 subjects per set.
limits: Not opened; URL is the proceedings index, not the paper.
agent_relevance: Size principle: prefer the narrowest rule that fits all examples. Cheap to put in S7.
